title: Kapapo, the endangered bird
titleCn: 鸮鹦鹉：濒危的新西兰夜行鹦鹉

paragraphs.text: The kakapo is a giant, green, flightless bird. A native of New Zealand, it had, indeed still has, a great deal of cultural and traditional significance to the Maori people who hunted it for food. It was plucked and eaten, and its feathers were individually woven into items of clothing, which were handed down through generations, creating a link with ancestors. Its skin was also used to create garments for the wives and daughters of leading chiefs.
Apart from the Maori people, in those early days, its only predator was the eagle, which was native to New Zealand.
The kakapo's feathers acted as camouflage, allowing them to blend in with their surroundings, and in this way, a balance was maintained.
Things changed in the eighteen hundreds when gold was discovered in New Zealand.

Along with Europeans seeking gold came animals like mice, which undermined the kakapo's natural environment and caused competition for food. By nineteen thirty-four, the main place kakapo could be found was in museums around the world.
Today, thanks to our kakapo recovery program, a unique system of monitoring and protection, there are now over one hundred kakapo living in New Zealand.

Firstly, let me tell you about the way in which we locate and monitor each kakapo. In the early days of research, the birds were located by dogs, which had been specially taught to do this. But these days, we are able to check up on all the birds by electronic means using a logging system known as the SNARC. Yes, an odd name, isn't it? Anyway, it's a black box that houses a computer. When we designed it, we realized it needed to be portable, so it could be carried around easily by any of the researchers or volunteers.

They take the SNARC and leave it in the specific part of the forest where the kakapo dwell. Each kakapo has already been fitted with a transmitter. Catching them so they can be fitted is relatively easy to do, as there are not many kakapo, and they are quite easy to trap. But actually fitting the transmitter can be quite a difficult task.

Originally, scientists attached the transmitter under one of its wings, but it could be easily dislodged. They had the same problem with the bird's foot. It is now attached to its leg, which has proven to be more successful. We can then use the transmitter to keep track of each kakapo, and the SNARC records the movements of birds within a ten-meter radius and stores the memory.

Even though we feel we are winning the fight against extinction, we have had some quite difficult moments in the past. For example, in nineteen ninety-eight, we discovered Codfish Island had experienced a sharp decline in kakapo numbers, so we went in and investigated. We thought that perhaps stoats had reached the island and were eating the kakapos. But when we got there, we found the place had literally become overrun by rats. This required drastic action. We were left with no alternative but to get rid of them. After getting volunteers to help with the removal of all wildlife from the island, including the kakapos, we arranged for a helicopter to start the huge job of spreading poison. Within a couple of months, we were able to safely reinstate the kakapo in their previous habitat on the island.

Another disaster occurred in two thousand and four on Chalky Island. Within a few days of establishing a colony of kakapo on the island, we found, to our dismay, that we had lost five birds. It was devastating. The reason for the deaths was unknown for months. We investigated a number of possible causes: bacteria in the soil, blood poisoning, even germs on the hands of the volunteers. It was later revealed to simply be a virus, but we weren't sure how to treat it.

Over a period of time, we were able to develop a treatment that worked, but we have since found that the recovering birds, which make up a large number of the kakapo population there, aren't fertile anymore, which is a devastating blow.
That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
